cues.text: A Weaver Turned Priest
Born in 1807 at Sallent, in Catalonia, Anthony trained as a weaver like his father.
In his early twenties, he decided to pursue the priesthood.
Poor health prevented him from joining the Jesuits as he originally hoped, and he was ordained a diocesan priest in 1835 instead.
A Popular Missionary Preacher
Anthony spent more than a decade traveling throughout Catalonia, preaching parish missions and retreats.
He developed a reputation for effective, deeply felt preaching that drew large crowds and sometimes provoked serious hostility.
His bishop sent him temporarily to the Canary Islands for safety.
Founding the Claretians
In July 1849, Anthony gathered five priest companions at the seminary of Vic and founded the Congregation of Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary .
Popularly known as the Claretians, the congregation was dedicated to preaching missions and popular Catholic instruction.
Around this same period, he took the additional name 'Mary' for himself.
Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba
At the recommendation of Queen Isabella II of Spain, Pope Pius IX appointed Anthony Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba in 1849.
Over the following six years he undertook exhaustive pastoral visitations across the diocese and reformed clerical discipline.
He validated thousands of previously irregular common-law marriages, preached openly against slavery, and founded schools, savings institutions, and technical training programs for the poor.
These reforms provoked such fierce opposition among vested colonial interests that an assassin once succeeded in wounding him with a knife.
Royal Confessor and Exile
Recalled to Spain in 1857 to serve as personal confessor to Queen Isabella II, Anthony accepted only on the strict condition that he live apart from the royal court.
He would attend only to hear the queen's confession and instruct the royal children, remaining free from ordinary court duties.
When revolution forced Isabella into exile in 1868, Anthony accompanied the royal party into exile in France as well.
Legacy
Anthony died in exile at the Cistercian abbey of Fontfroide, near Narbonne, in 1870, having spent his final years continuing to write and preach to the exiled Spanish community.

Canonized in 1950, he is remembered as a tireless missionary preacher and social reformer whose Claretian order, still active on all six continents, carries forward his particular combination of popular preaching, education, and the printed word.
